correctness.rationale: For the stated rooted, vertex-only cover of an individual shortest path, the distance from the root along any covering path increases by one per step. Shortest paths in H(d,q) change each differing coordinate exactly once, giving the universal d+1 vertex bound. In the nonbinary case a path that switches each coordinate between two letters neither equal to the corresponding root letter has length d, is shortest, and has all d+1 vertices in the outer sphere, so each covering path can meet it only once. In the binary case every edge joins adjacent root layers; a root geodesic to the nearer endpoint extended by that edge covers the pair, permitting disjoint blocks of two plus at most one singleton. Conversely start with floor(d/2) disagreements and flip alternating agreeing and disagreeing coordinates, with one extra agreeing flip if d is odd. Each coordinate is flipped only once, all d+1 vertices are in two adjacent layers, and each rooted path covers at most two. These arguments hold at every root and include d=1 and length-zero geodesics. An independent exact finite check (`python3 -B /workspace/branches/bounded_review_checks.py 1`) obtained the packaged histograms on 7210 geodesic vertex sets by enumerating maximum antichains, not by the packaged set-cover DP. For that check, u precedes v iff every nonroot letter of u agrees with v in its coordinate; rooted paths intersect the tested path in chains, each chain extends to a rooted geodesic, and Dilworth gives the exact width. The packaged verifier was inspected, not executed; no finite check is needed to extrapolate the proof.

value.rationale: This evaluates a naturally motivated graph invariant on a canonical product family, showing exactly how a one-letter increase can change worst-case complexity from about half the diameter to the maximum possible. The result provides reusable explicit witnesses and explains which metric feature—two-layer alternation versus staying in one layer—drives the transition.
